The session begins.

The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.

The tiefling lad catches the look on its way back from the barrel and gives you a quick, crooked smile, the kind people give when they've seen that look before. He falls in beside you in the line, rope sling hitched up on his shoulder. Up close he's younger than you thought, sixteen at most, with horns filed blunt and a coat cut for someone broader.

"Tamsin, ser. Just Tamsin." He nods at your pack, sizing it up like a man pricing fish. "Three coppers to carry that up to the Lower City, ser. If it's heavier than it looks, five. I'll tell you which once I've lifted it, honest."

The line shuffles forward a step. A sailor at the barrel swears, and the card-woman laughs. She doesn't call after you again, but when you glance over she's still watching, cards moving under her fingers without her looking down. At your boots the cat has gone very flat and still, its ears turned towards the barrel.

"A clean inn," Tamsin goes on, counting on his fingers. "Widow Penhale's, ser, on Cook Street by the Wide. That's the big market square. Sheets get washed, the door bolts, and nobody sells your boots while you sleep. Five silver a night with supper, ser. Maybe less if you stay the tenday and look sad at her. The Elfsong's nicer, but you pay for the ghost." He hesitates, choosing his words. "The Lady, though. Her house is up top, the Lady's Hall, behind the inner wall. The Watch shuts the gates at this hour, ser. You'll not get up there before morning, and even then they look at you first." He gives a little shrug. "Down here people just throw a copper in the harbour and hope."

The merchant ahead of you finishes at the table and hurries off. The broad sergeant under the Fist awning dips his pen, wipes the ink-stained thumb on his tabard, and looks up at you with no interest at all.

"Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep." His eyes flick to Tamsin and back. "He with you?"

Tamsin's face does something quick and pleased when you say "five," as if he had expected to be argued down to three. "Five, ser. Done." He crouches, slides the rope sling under your pack and lifts it. He grunts once and doesn't mention it.

The sergeant writes as you talk. His pen scratches *Worgen* into the ledger, then stops on the last letter. He looks up at you properly for the first time, a short, flat look like a man checking a coin, and then back down. "Zaranda's army." It isn't a question, and he doesn't sound impressed. "Lady's Hall's up top. Gates open at dawn. Watch'll want to know why." He writes *Penhale's* in a cramped hand. Under the heel of his left hand, half under the ledger's edge, there's a scrap of paper, and from across the trestle you watch him add one more short line to it. He doesn't hide it, and he doesn't make a show of it either. Then his thumb comes down over it.

"The lad carries. Doesn't wander." He's looking at Tamsin when he says it. Tamsin's eyes are fixed on the cobbles. "Go on. Next."

While the pen was still moving you sent your question down the bond, and the cat's answer comes the way it always does, not in words so much as a nudge against your senses:

*Smell.* The quay pours in through it: tar, fish guts, wet rope, sailors' sweat, frying oil, the stale wine on the man at the barrel. Then a gap where the woman should be. It's like a spot on a page where the ink won't take. *Everyone smells. She doesn't.* A pause, and the fur along its spine lifts against your boot. *Wrong.*

Then it's just a cat again, sitting very upright and still not looking away from the barrel.

As Tamsin leads you off the landing towards the street that climbs from the quay, the way runs past the warehouse door. The sailors are counting out coppers for another hand. The card-woman doesn't look up from her shuffle, but she speaks loud enough to carry.

"Penhale's does a decent fish stew, Tethyr." The cards ripple from one hand to the other. "Seat'll keep. Ask anyone on the quay for Mirela."

Tamsin walks a little faster. Ahead of you the street climbs between shuttered stalls and lit windows towards the Wide and Cook Street, about a quarter-hour's walk, he says.

*Stay with me,* goes down the bond, *and no investigating her alone.*

The answer comes back short and warm, the cat's version of agreeing: *Here. With you.* It trots on at your heel with its tail up again, though twice in the first fifty feet one ear swivels back towards the quay, as if it hasn't fully made up its mind.

The street climbs away from the water. The harbour noise falls behind the first row of warehouses, and in its place come shutters banging closed, a dog barking somewhere, and a woman calling a child in for the night. Tamsin keeps the pack steady on his shoulder and doesn't answer straight away when you ask. He walks another dozen steps before he speaks.

"Both, ser. Bit of both." He glances back down the slope, then at you. "Sergeant Brannick's not bad, as Fist go. But when he says *doesn't wander* to a lad like me, he means if anything goes missing off that quay tonight, he knows whose door to knock on. And the Seatower's not somewhere you come back from the same." His eyes drift down to the cobbles and come back up. "So I walk quick and I keep my hands where he can see them, ser. That's all that was."

He shifts the sling and lowers his voice, though there's nobody near enough to hear.

"Mirela, though. I don't know anything bad about her, not really, ser. She's been on that barrel since before the rains. Deals fair, far as anyone can tell, and she's always laughing. Only the sailors have a saying about her table: it's a fine table to lose at and a bad one to leave rich." He shrugs, a little embarrassed, like a boy repeating a ghost story. "Ned Coyle won eleven gold off her one night, all in one go. Bought the whole Mermaid a round. Next tenday his barge went over on the river, empty water, no rocks, no wind. Ned lived, but the cargo didn't, and it wasn't his. There's others. Nobody says it's her doing, ser. They just don't win big there anymore, and they still sit down." He frowns. "And she'd got your name and your bed off the sergeant's table before you'd finished saying it. She does that with everybody. It's a bit much, I think, ser."

He says it plainly. As far as you can tell from his face, he believes every word, and the thing he's scared of is the Fist.

Up ahead, the street opens towards a wide lamplit space with the shapes of market stalls, covered for the night: the Wide. Tamsin nods towards a narrower lane leading off its far side. "Cook Street's just there, ser. Penhale's is the green door. Five minutes."

Tamsin glances sideways at you when you say it, as if checking it's a kindness and not a test. Then he ducks his head. "Straight to Penhale's, ser. That's what happened." He says it quietly, the way you'd repeat an address you mean to remember, and shifts the pack higher on his shoulder.

The Wide is mostly empty at this hour. Covered stalls sit in rows under the lamps, and a pair of Fist men lean on a water trough at the far end, talking with their helmets off. Halfway across, the cat stops at an iron drain grate set in the cobbles. It doesn't sniff it. It stands over it, very still, head low, looking down between the bars at nothing you can see. Then it shakes itself, catches up at a trot and walks pressed to your boot for the rest of the way, close enough that you feel it against your ankle with every step.

Cook Street is narrow and smells of old woodsmoke and onions. The green door is halfway down, its paint flaking but the step scrubbed pale. A lamp is still burning behind the shutters on the ground floor. Tamsin sets your pack down on the step, carefully, and stands back to wait.

You knock. For a while nothing happens. Then a small hatch at head height slides open, and a woman's face fills it: sixty or so, grey hair pinned flat for sleep, a shawl held closed at the throat. She looks at you, then down at Tamsin, then at the cat.

"Tamsin. Bit late for you to be bringing me anyone." She doesn't sound angry about it, only tired. Her eyes come back to you. "Room's five silver the night, supper in it, and you've missed supper. There's stew left in the pot. It'll be warm in a quarter-hour if you don't mind waiting." A short pause while she takes in the cloak and the crossbow. "Door's bolted at midnight and I don't unbolt it for anyone till the bread's in. The cat can stay if it keeps off the bolsters." The hatch stays open. "You want it, or are you just looking?"

The hatch slides shut, a bolt scrapes, then a second one, and the green door opens on a narrow hall that smells of onions, lye soap and the last of a peat fire. Widow Penhale holds a candle in one hand and her shawl closed with the other. She takes the five silver without counting it twice, which in its way is counting it once, and drops it into her apron pocket.

"Worgen." She nods once, like she's filing the name somewhere. "Top of the stairs, second door. Pot's on the hook."

Tamsin closes his hand around the five coppers fast, the way you'd catch something about to roll away, and lets the rope sling slide off his shoulder so you can take the pack. When you ask if he's eaten, he opens his mouth, shuts it again, and looks at the widow, not at you.

"I'm all right, ser. Honest, I—" His stomach answers before he does, loud in the quiet hall. The tips of his ears go dark. "...Haven't, ser. Not since the noon boats."

The widow looks at him over the candle for a long moment. Her face doesn't soften, but she doesn't say no either.

"There's enough for two bowls if nobody wants seconds." She turns to you. "Two coppers for his. He eats in the kitchen, not on my step, and he's gone before the bolt goes on at midnight." Then, to Tamsin, flatter: "Boots off the bench."

The cat has already slipped past everyone's ankles and is sitting at the foot of the stairs, tail curled round its feet, looking back down the hall at the open door and the dark street beyond it. After a moment it decides the street can wait and walks off towards the smell of stew.

Tamsin is waiting for your answer, cap half off already.

Widow Penhale takes the two coppers off your palm and drops them into the apron pocket with the silver. "Kitchen's through the back." She goes ahead with the candle.

The kitchen is small and warm. There's a scrubbed table, two benches, a peat fire banked low under the hook, and a black pot that has started to tick as it heats. Bunches of onions hang from a beam, and someone's mended stockings are drying on a string across the chimney corner. You set your pack down by the end of the bench. Tamsin perches on the very edge of the bench opposite, feet flat on the floor, boots well clear of the wood.

He blinks when you tell him to drop the "ser." "Right. Yes, s—" His mouth catches it halfway. "James." He tries it again under his breath, like a coin he's not sure is good, and his ears go dark at the tips again. "Feels like cheek, saying it. But all right."

The widow stirs the pot, tastes it off the spoon and frowns at it.

While she does, you reach down the bond. The cat is under the table, sitting by your boot with its tail wrapped round its feet, and it answers in pieces, the way it always does.

*Stones. Under the stones.* The Wide comes back to you, cold iron bars and wet dark below them, the smell of drain water and old leaves. Under that is something with no smell at all. *A pull.* It's the feeling of a mouse scratching behind a wall that you can hear and can't find, only it isn't moving and it isn't a mouse. It just sits there and pulls, the way a fire pulls at a cold hand. *Not water. Not rat. Not anything.* Then a tilt, like a head turning: back across the square and down the hill, towards the harbour but not all the way to the water. *That way.* A pause. *Here too. Small.* Even in this kitchen it's still there, faint, at the back of the cat's attention like a sound in the next room.

Then, honestly, the way a cat is honest: *Don't like it.* And right on top of that: *Want it.*

Widow Penhale ladles stew into two wooden bowls. It's thick with fish and barley and smells of pepper. She sets them down with a heel of bread each and two spoons. "Bowls in the basin after. Bolt's at midnight." She looks at Tamsin. "Twenty minutes, then you're out." She picks up her candle and goes, and you hear the stairs creak under her.

Tamsin waits for you to pick up your spoon first. Then he eats like someone trying very hard to look as if he isn't starving, and failing.

Under the table the cat leans its weight against your ankle and sends one more thing, quieter, almost a question:

*When you sleep, I go and look? Come back.*

*Not alone,* you send down the bond. *If it can pull at you, I want to be there when you find it. We'll look together.*

For a moment the cat doesn't answer at all. Its tail flicks once against your boot, then again, a short, put-out twitch. Then it comes: *Together.* It's grudging, but it's agreeing. Under that the pull is still there at the back of its attention, a sound in the next room that nobody's going to go and check. The cat lies down across your feet as if to make sure neither of you goes anywhere, and starts washing a forepaw with great concentration.

The stew is good. It's peppery and thick, and the fish was fresh this morning. You get a few spoonfuls down before you speak, and by then Tamsin's bowl is already half empty.

At the offer of work he stops with the spoon halfway up. He puts it down, and then he seems to realise he's put it down and picks it up again.

"Tomorrow? The Lady's Hall?" He thinks fast, and you can watch him do the sums. "I can get you to the gate in the inner wall, s— James. Right to it, the quick way, not round by the Wide. But I'll not get through it myself, likely. The Watch up there don't like the look of me." He touches one blunt horn without seeming to notice he's done it. "So it'd be the walk there, and I wait at the bottom in case they turn you round and you want somewhere else. A silver?" He hears himself say it and his ears darken. "No, that's too much for a walk. Six coppers. Six is fair."

He scrapes the bowl, quick and thorough, and looks over at the kitchen door where the widow went out.

"Mistress Penhale draws the bolt when the bread's in, about sunup. I'll be on the step." He hesitates. "Maybe a bit after sunup. I've got someone to see home first thing, and then I'm free. Not long. Is that all right?"

Upstairs a floorboard creaks. The fire in the grate has burned down to a dull red. There can't be more than a few minutes left before midnight.

Tamsin grins at "more work and more pay," a quick grin he can't quite stop. "Then I'll hope you get turned round, s— James." He hears what he's just said and goes red to the horns. "No. I don't mean that. I'll be on the step."

He scrapes the last of his bowl clean with the bread and hands it to you before you can reach for it. You set both bowls in the stone basin under the window, where a skin of cold water is already waiting. In the hall he pulls his cap down, pauses with his hand on the latch as if he's about to say something more, then just nods and slips out into Cook Street. Behind him the street is dark and empty except for one lamp at the corner. His footsteps go quickly towards the Wide and are gone.

The stairs creak. Widow Penhale comes halfway down in a nightcap with the candle, looks past you at the closed door, then comes the rest of the way and draws both bolts with a sound like a full stop. "That's midnight." She looks at the kitchen, sees the bowls in the basin, and says nothing about it, which you suspect is her way of approving. Then she goes back up.

Your room is the second door at the top of the stairs. It's narrow, with a sloped ceiling, a bed with a clean grey blanket, a washstand and a jug, and a shutter latched against the night. It smells faintly of lye. There's a wooden bar on the inside of the door. It drops into its bracket with a solid knock.

The cat comes in ahead of you and inspects everything: under the bed, behind the washstand, the gap under the shutter. When you set the pack down at the foot of the bed it goes to sniff it the way it sniffs everything. It stops at the flap of the side pocket where you keep your papers, stays there a moment with its nose an inch from the leather, then turns away and jumps up onto the far end of the bed, as far from the pack as the bed allows. It turns round twice and settles with its back to it.

Through the bond you get nothing clear from it, just a sort of shrug: *Not there.*

You sit down on the bed. The blanket is rough, the mattress is better than a ship's bunk, and the house goes quiet around you.

*Velen, Flamerule, '94*

*James,*

*Fenn says he saw you at the Gull, so this goes there on the chance, and if it finds you somewhere else, well, it found you.*

*The Weathercocks are done. We paid off at Zazesspur after the Amnian wagons, and when it came to signing again nobody picked up the pen, me least of all. Nobody quarrelled about it. We were just tired, and the wagons don't get any lighter. Odessa's married a cooper, if you'll believe that, and is learning to make barrels so she can tell him he does it wrong. Little Pell went home to his mother's farm outside Ithmong and writes to say the goats respect him. I've kept the boat and I take fish and the odd passenger along the coast, and it's enough. Most nights it's more than enough.*

*Now the part I've been putting off for two pages.*

*I know the forty's gone. Fenn told me how, and where, and I didn't need telling. Don't send it. I don't want it, and I'd only think of where you'd got it. If you want to pay me, stop. That's the whole price, and I know it's dearer than forty.*

*I'm not writing to scold you. You carried Pell out of the Hollow on your back with your own leg cut open, and you never once made a thing of it. A man who'll do that is worth more than whatever's on the table, and the table's never going to see it. I wish you would.*

*If you go north, and I think you might, since you always go where the money's loud, Bram Tolley is in Baldur's Gate. He lost the eye at Saradush, you'll remember, and he's bosun on the river cogs there now. He drinks at the Blushing Mermaid on the quay, mostly in the corner by the door so nobody comes at him on his blind side. Tell him I sent you. Tell him he still owes me a boot. He'll know.*

*Write if you like. If you don't, I'll take it you're well and busy.*

*Look after yourself, you great fool.*

*— Rhoswen*

---

Below the name, smaller and in a hurry, as if she nearly didn't add it:

*The boat's called the Second Chance. Odessa named her. Don't laugh.*

That's all of it. The candle gutters in a draught from the shutter and steadies. Downstairs the house has gone fully quiet, without even the tick of the stew pot, and somewhere out past Cook Street a dog barks twice and gives up.

At the far end of the bed the cat has its eyes half open, fixed on the pack and the pocket you left unbuckled, not on you or the letter.

Nothing else happens before dawn unless you want it to. The widow unbolts the door when the bread's in, and Tamsin said he'd be on the step a little after sunup.

James sits a while with the letter open on his knee, his thumb beside Rhoswen's name. The candle leans in the draught and straightens. At the far end of the bed one of the cat's ears turns towards him when he speaks, and then turns back to the pocket.

He folds the letter along its old creases and puts it aside.

*You've been watching my papers. Is something wrong with the note?*

The cat doesn't answer at once. It gets up, walks the length of the blanket, and stops a foot short of the pack, where the bed ends. It doesn't come any closer.

James draws the note out and smooths it flat on the washstand beside the clay dish.

It's good paper, much better than what's written on it. It's heavy and cream-coloured, cut clean at the edges, the kind of sheet a counting-room or a great house keeps in a drawer. The ink is brown-black oak-gall. Someone wrote fast with it, pressed too hard in places and blotted it without waiting. A pale ring near the bottom shows where a wine cup was set down on it once.

*I, Peregrin Vane, promise to pay the bearer of this note four hundred gold pieces on presentation, against the account of House Vane at the Counting House of Baldur's Gate.*

Under that is the signature. *Peregrin* is clear, but *Vane* runs downhill, and the last stroke drags off the paper as if the pen kept going after the hand had stopped caring. There is no date and no witness. There's just the name, the sum and the building.

While he reads, the cat's answer comes down the bond in pieces.

The memory comes back from a long way off, from Tethyr and the war years, before the companies. There was a hedge-priest of the Lady who followed the camps and blessed dice for a copper a throw. On one wet night he talked more than usual.

Beshaba's sign is antlers, he said. Black antlers on a red field. Her people don't paint her face. Farmers nail antlers over a door to keep her away, and sometimes over a neighbour's door to bring her down on him. James saw that once himself in a burned village outside Ithmong, a rack of antlers left on a gatepost, and nobody would go through that gate. The Maid of Misfortune doesn't weep in any picture he knows. When anyone shows her at all, she's laughing.

Tymora doesn't weep either. On every coin and shrine he can call to mind, she wears the smile that's worn down on the coin round his own neck.

The priest had an older story, though, and told it like a man not quite sure he should. Long ago there was only one Lady of luck. In some disaster before anyone's grandmother was born she was torn in two, the smile and the frown, and the two halves have been sisters and enemies ever since. *One coin,* the priest called them. *You can't have the face without the back of it.* The soldiers had a habit that came from it. When they tossed for a bad duty they didn't call heads or tails. They called *Lady* or *Maid.*

He remembers one more thing the priest said, because it was the part that frightened the young soldiers. The Maid doesn't strike the man who's losing. She follows the one who's just won big, a little behind him and patient, and one day his luck turns sour. The camps called it the Maid's toll.

So he knows plenty, and none of it is quite this face. It has the Lady's brow and hair, but neither sister is ever shown crying. There's a plainer reading too, and a sensible man would weigh it. Some southern houses put a weeping face on their seals and papers for a year after a death in the family. A patriar house might do the same, and a mill would put whatever the house paid for into the sheet.

Then something quieter. It isn't a smell or anything to do with the coin. It's her. *She stops.* As the coin slaps onto the back of Callis's hand, the cat gives him what it noticed: her shoulders lock, and for a breath nothing about her moves, the way a mouse goes still in the open. *Every time.* Then her hand lifts, she smiles, and the stillness is gone.

He watches for a while himself. Reading people across a table used to be his whole living, and this needs no cards. A wool-trader pays his silver, and the coin goes up and comes down. *She smiles on you.* A girl with a basket of eggs gets a copper toss for luck at a reduced rate. *She smiles on you.* A pair of carters get one each. A sellsword's widow, by her black armband, gets one too. Over the quarter-hour he counts eleven tosses. Every call is the same, warm and unhurried. Every time she looks under her palm for that one beat, and every time the coin goes back into her sleeve before anyone gets a look at it. Nobody asks to see it. People who've just been told the Lady smiles on them don't ask for proof.

A man who has sat across from coin-tossers in a hundred camps knows a fair coin doesn't come up the same eleven times running. It might, once in a long life of watching. He has also seen enough honest tossers to know that the calls almost never come out wrong *that* way, in the buyer's favour every time, from the house's own hand.

Inside the hall the queue at the offering table thins. The acolyte's pen moves and stops, moves and stops. The last giver, a stout woman in a good cloak, presses something heavy into the slotted box and goes away happy.

I enjoyed this session. James felt like someone with a past and a dangerous obligation, not just a warlock waiting for a quest marker.

**What worked**
- **The people.** Tamsin and Widow Penhale were convincing without needing elaborate introductions. Negotiating a porter’s fee, buying him supper, and respecting the widow’s rules gave me room to establish James through choices.
- **The cat’s communication.** Sensations, smells, and simple wants made it feel like a familiar rather than a narrator handing me answers. “Don’t like it. Want it.” was particularly good.
- **Rhoswen’s letter.** This was the strongest emotional moment. It made James’s gambling history hurt, gave him relationships beyond the goddess, and offered a useful contact without becoming a quest briefing.
- **The connected clues.** Mirela’s absent scent, the pull beneath the streets, and the note’s watermark gave me reasons to investigate. The acolyte asking for the goddess’s actual words was an excellent stopping point.
- **Freedom to be cautious.** I could decline the cards, avoid sending the cat into danger alone, and seek counsel without the game forcing an encounter.

**What broke**
- **The starting records weren’t applied consistently.** The letter was missing until I quoted the campaign file. The opening sheet also changed Arcana to History and imposed attunement on uncommon items despite the campaign’s explicit exception. Some other changes may have been attempts to correct the supplied sheet to standard 5e, but those should be flagged rather than silently substituted.
- **The rest and clock tracking were unreliable.** A five-hour-forty-minute sleep was labelled a long rest despite the eight-hour rule. Evening also became nearly midnight surprisingly quickly relative to the listed travel and conversation times.
- **The failed out-of-game message interrupted play.** The correction was handled well once it reached the GM, but having to resend it was friction.

**What was missing**
- **More forward movement.** An entire session covered arrival, lodging, and reaching the first substantive conversation at the temple. I liked those scenes, but repeated small exchanges and travel descriptions stretched them. I’d keep the important choices and compress the transitions.
- **A little more initiative from the world.** Nearly every interaction waited for my next question or confirmation. NPCs could sometimes finish an arrangement or volunteer the next useful detail without another turn.
- **An early glimpse of the promised adventure.** I don’t need the heist revealed immediately, but I’d like a concrete objective or meaningful opportunity soon. So far the experience is an atmospheric mystery rather than the beginnings of assembling a crew.

One caution: not every memorable person or object needs to feel ominous. The mundane kindness and old-company history made the supernatural clues more effective.

Overall, I’d gladly continue. Keep the character work and sensory clues; tighten the pacing and make the campaign records dependable.

Tamsin keeps the pack steady on his shoulder and doesn't answer straight away when you ask. He walks another dozen steps before he speaks.

"Both, ser. Bit of both." He glances back down the slope, then at you. "Sergeant Brannick's not bad, as Fist go. But when he says *doesn't wander* to a lad like me, he means if anything goes missing off that quay tonight, he knows whose door to knock on. "Mirela, though. I don't know anything bad about her, not really, ser. She's been on that barrel since before the rains. Deals fair, far as anyone can tell, and she's always laughing. "Ned Coyle won eleven gold off her one night, all in one go. Bought the whole Mermaid a round. Next tenday his barge went over on the river, empty water, no rocks, no wind. turns.reply:
A tallow stub stands in a clay dish on the washstand. It takes three strikes of the tinderbox before the wick catches, and then the room is small and yellow and full of moving shadows.

When you open the side pocket the cat lifts its head at the far end of the bed. It doesn't get up. It watches your hand go in past the pay slip and the stiff, folded note, and it lowers its chin onto its paws again only once your hand comes out holding the letter.

The letter has been folded and unfolded more than once. The paper is cheap and soft at the creases, with a tide mark along one edge where it got wet in somebody's satchel. The wax is broken. It was a blob of red pressed with a little weathercock, the old company seal, and half of it still clings to the flap. The hand is square and upright and pushes hard into the paper, the way she always wrote, like she was angry at the pen.

---

*Velen, Flamerule, '94*

*James,*

*Fenn says he saw you at the Gull, so this goes there on the chance, and if it finds you somewhere else, well, it found you.*

*The Weathercocks are done. We paid off at Zazesspur after the Amnian wagons, and when it came to signing again nobody picked up the pen, me least of all. Nobody quarrelled about it. We were just tired, and the wagons don't get any lighter. Odessa's married a cooper, if you'll believe that, and is learning to make barrels so she can tell him he does it wrong. Little Pell went home to his mother's farm outside Ithmong and writes to say the goats respect him. I've kept the boat and I take fish and the odd passenger along the coast, and it's enough. Most nights it's more than enough.*

*Now the part I've been putting off for two pages.*

*I know the forty's gone. Fenn told me how, and where, and I didn't need telling. Don't send it. I don't want it, and I'd only think of where you'd got it. If you want to pay me, stop. That's the whole price, and I know it's dearer than forty.*

*I'm not writing to scold you. You carried Pell out of the Hollow on your back with your own leg cut open, and you never once made a thing of it. A man who'll do that is worth more than whatever's on the table, and the table's never going to see it. I wish you would.*

*If you go north, and I think you might, since you always go where the money's loud, Bram Tolley is in Baldur's Gate. He lost the eye at Saradush, you'll remember, and he's bosun on the river cogs there now. He drinks at the Blushing Mermaid on the quay, mostly in the corner by the door so nobody comes at him on his blind side. Tell him I sent you. Tell him he still owes me a boot. He'll know.*

*Write if you like. If you don't, I'll take it you're well and busy.*

*Look after yourself, you great fool.*

*— Rhoswen*

---

Below the name, smaller and in a hurry, as if she nearly didn't add it:

*The boat's called the Second Chance. Odessa named her. Don't laugh.*

That's all of it. The candle gutters in a draught from the shutter and steadies. Downstairs the house has gone fully quiet, without even the tick of the stew pot, and somewhere out past Cook Street a dog barks twice and gives up.

At the far end of the bed the cat has its eyes half open, fixed on the pack and the pocket you left unbuckled, not on you or the letter.

Nothing else happens before dawn unless you want it to. The widow unbolts the door when the bread's in, and Tamsin said he'd be on the step a little after sunup.

turns.reply:
James sits a while with the letter open on his knee, his thumb beside Rhoswen's name. The candle leans in the draught and straightens. At the far end of the bed one of the cat's ears turns towards him when he speaks, and then turns back to the pocket.

He folds the letter along its old creases and puts it aside.

*You've been watching my papers. Is something wrong with the note?*

The cat doesn't answer at once. It gets up, walks the length of the blanket, and stops a foot short of the pack, where the bed ends. It doesn't come any closer.

James draws the note out and smooths it flat on the washstand beside the clay dish.

It's good paper, much better than what's written on it. It's heavy and cream-coloured, cut clean at the edges, the kind of sheet a counting-room or a great house keeps in a drawer. The ink is brown-black oak-gall. Someone wrote fast with it, pressed too hard in places and blotted it without waiting. A pale ring near the bottom shows where a wine cup was set down on it once.

*I, Peregrin Vane, promise to pay the bearer of this note four hundred gold pieces on presentation, against the account of House Vane at the Counting House of Baldur's Gate.*

Under that is the signature. *Peregrin* is clear, but *Vane* runs downhill, and the last stroke drags off the paper as if the pen kept going after the hand had stopped caring. There is no date and no witness. There's just the name, the sum and the building.

While he reads, the cat's answer comes down the bond in pieces.

*Smell.* Paper, ink, old wine, the sour sweat of someone's palm that sat flat on this sheet for a long time. Ordinary things. Then under them, very faint, there's the gap again where a smell should be, the same nothing that sits under the stones on the Wide. *Same as the pull.* There's a pause, and the cat's fur shifts against itself as if a hand had stroked it from tail to ears. *Same. Backwards.*

Then, quite firmly: *Not on the bed.*

James leans closer to the candle to read the blotted part of the signature, and the flame comes near the sheet's edge. Where the light gets through the thin margin there is something in the paper itself, a paler patch inside the cream that isn't on the surface. It's a curve, like the line of a cheek. Lying flat on the washstand it fades back into the sheet as soon as he moves his head. Held up between his eye and the flame, it would show.

The cat sits down at the edge of the blanket and waits to see what he does with it.

I hold the note up to the candlelight, well clear of the flame, to examine the pale image in the paper. I draw Tymora’s coin out on its cord beside it for comparison.

*Backwards how?* I ask the cat. *Does it push you away where the thing beneath the stones pulls?*
turns.reply:
James tilts the sheet towards the candle, keeping its edge a hand's width from the flame, and the light comes through the paper from behind.

The pale patch fills in. It's a woman's face set inside a plain ring, with tiny regular nicks around the ring like the milled edge of a coin. She faces him full on. Her hair is drawn back from a high brow, and her eyes are cast down. The mouth turns down at the corners, and from each eye a thin pale line runs down the cheek nearly to the jaw. She's weeping. There's no mistaking it once he's seen it. The ink of *Peregrin Vane, four hundred gold pieces* lies across her face like writing on a window.

He brings Tymora's coin out on its cord and holds it beside the sheet. It's the coin he's turned over in his fingers a thousand times. Years of thumbs have worn the Lady's face smooth, but the smile is still there, a small sideways one, as if she's just heard something funny. In the candlelight the two faces are close enough to make him look twice: the brow, the hair drawn back, the shape of the cheek he saw first. Or it's only that every face cut for a coin ends up a little like every other. One of them smiles, and the one in the paper doesn't. When he lowers the note the face fades back into plain cream, and only good paper and bad handwriting are left.

*Backwards how? Does it push you away where the thing beneath the stones pulls?*

The cat thinks about it. Its tail moves once along the blanket.

*Push. Little.* Then comes a sensation instead of a word: the warmth on one side of a fire, the side you lean towards, and then the cold at its back where the draught goes out under the door. *Stones-thing, I lean in. Paper, cold side.* A pause. *Same fire.*

Its eyes move to the coin on its cord, and the bond warms a little, plain and easy. *That one smells of you.*

Then it looks back at the note in his hand, and its ears go flat for a moment. *Not on the bed,* it says again, as if he might have forgotten.

The candle has burned down a finger's width. Outside the shutter Cook Street is silent. It's past the middle of the night and still hours till the bread goes in.

turns.message:
“Not on the bed. Understood.”

I fold the note and stow it separately from the letter and pay slip, in the pack at the foot of the washstand. Before putting out the candle, I try to recall whether I’ve seen that weeping face in religious imagery—particularly anything connected with Tymora or her sister, Beshaba.
turns.reply:
James folds the note along its fresh crease and puts it away by itself in the pack at the foot of the washstand, apart from Rhoswen's letter and the pay slip. The cat watches the pack's flap go down. Then it turns round once on the blanket and settles, its back to the washstand now and not to the bed.

He sits with the candle a moment longer and tries to remember where else he has seen that face.

The memory comes back from a long way off, from Tethyr and the war years, before the companies. There was a hedge-priest of the Lady who followed the camps and blessed dice for a copper a throw. On one wet night he talked more than usual.

Beshaba's sign is antlers, he said. Black antlers on a red field. Her people don't paint her face. Farmers nail antlers over a door to keep her away, and sometimes over a neighbour's door to bring her down on him. James saw that once himself in a burned village outside Ithmong, a rack of antlers left on a gatepost, and nobody would go through that gate. The Maid of Misfortune doesn't weep in any picture he knows. When anyone shows her at all, she's laughing.

Tymora doesn't weep either. On every coin and shrine he can call to mind, she wears the smile that's worn down on the coin round his own neck.

The priest had an older story, though, and told it like a man not quite sure he should. Long ago there was only one Lady of luck. In some disaster before anyone's grandmother was born she was torn in two, the smile and the frown, and the two halves have been sisters and enemies ever since. *One coin,* the priest called them. *You can't have the face without the back of it.* The soldiers had a habit that came from it. When they tossed for a bad duty they didn't call heads or tails. They called *Lady* or *Maid.*

He remembers one more thing the priest said, because it was the part that frightened the young soldiers. The Maid doesn't strike the man who's losing. She follows the one who's just won big, a little behind him and patient, and one day his luck turns sour. The camps called it the Maid's toll.

So he knows plenty, and none of it is quite this face. It has the Lady's brow and hair, but neither sister is ever shown crying. There's a plainer reading too, and a sensible man would weigh it. Some southern houses put a weeping face on their seals and papers for a year after a death in the family. A patriar house might do the same, and a mill would put whatever the house paid for into the sheet.

The candle has burned low. James pinches it out, and the room goes dark. At the end of the bed the cat sighs the way cats do, long, as if the whole business has been a great imposition, and goes still.

Nothing more happens before dawn unless you want it to. The widow draws the bolts when the bread's in, and Tamsin will be on the step a little after sunup.

James tucks the coin under his shirt, where it lies warm against his breastbone, and lies down under the grey blanket. The note stays in the pack by the washstand. The cat waits until he's still, then walks up the blanket and settles in the crook behind his knees. It has its back to the washstand, and nothing more comes from it.

The house creaks and goes quiet. Once in the night a cart goes past on Cook Street with a loose wheel. Once the cat lifts its head at something on the roof, decides it's a pigeon, and lies down again. James sleeps the way soldiers learn to, all at once and without dreams he remembers.

He wakes to the smell of bread.

Grey light is coming through the gap under the shutter. Below him a door bangs, and the bolts go back one after the other. Outside, Cook Street is waking up: a broom on a step, a woman calling to another across the lane, the clop of a donkey. Farther off, towards the Wide, a crier from Baldur's Mouth is working through the morning's news in a voice like a gull's. *Grain up two coppers the sack at the Wide. Council to hear the Black Network's road-toll offer at the tenday's end. A hoist down at the Grey Harbour yards, rope parted under a full load, one man crushed, Fist asking questions.* Then he goes back to grain prices.

Not long after, there's a knock on his door. It's three short raps, the knock of someone with bread in the oven and no time for a fourth.

"Worgen." It's Widow Penhale. "Your lad's on my step. He's been there since the bolts went back." There's a short pause. "I'll not have him sitting there all morning. People talk."

Her footsteps start away down the stairs, then stop.

"There's new bread. A copper the loaf, butter's another. You want it, or not?"

The cat is already up on the sill with its nose pushed into the gap under the shutter, tail twitching, watching the street.

“Two loaves and butter, please. I’ll be right down.”

I wash, dress, and gather my gear, checking that the note is safely tucked away separately from my other papers. Downstairs I pay four coppers and take the bread out to Tamsin, offering him a loaf.

“Morning. Ready to show us the way?” I nod to the cat. “All three of us.”
turns.reply:
Widow Penhale's voice comes back up the stairs. "Two and butter. Four coppers." The steps go on down.

The water in the jug is cold enough to take the sleep out of James's face. He dresses and buckles on the studded leather, then the old regimental cloak, and checks his gear the way a soldier does before a march: crossbow slung, rod, pouch, bolts. Last of all he checks the papers. The pay slip and Rhoswen's letter go back into the side pocket. The note stays by itself in the inside of the pack, folded along its crease. The cat watches the pack's flap come down, jumps off the sill and is at the door before him.

The kitchen is hot from the oven and smells so strongly of new bread that the onions on the beam don't stand a chance. Two loaves sit cooling on the scrubbed table with a thumb of butter beside each on a square of waxed paper. James counts four coppers into the widow's hand. She drops them into her apron pocket without looking and goes straight back to the oven with the peel.

"Bar's off your door when you go out, the room's kept. Five silver again tonight if you're stopping." She slides another tray in. "You're stopping?"

She doesn't wait long for an answer. A pan behind her needs turning, and she turns it.

Outside, Cook Street is grey and damp. The sun isn't over the roofs yet, but the sky above them has gone pale. A man on a ladder at the corner is pinching out the last lamp. Two doors down a girl is beating a rug against the wall as if it owes her money.

Tamsin is sitting on the very end of the step with his knees together, as far from the door as he can get and still be on the step. He scrambles up when James comes out, pulling his cap off. His coat is damp across the shoulders, as if he walked through the river mist to get here.

He looks at the loaf held out to him and doesn't take it right away.

"That's— you don't have to, s—" He shuts his mouth, takes a breath, and tries again. "Thank you, James." He takes the loaf in both hands. He breaks off one end and eats that, and the rest goes carefully into the inside of his coat with the butter on top, wrapped up. He doesn't say who it's for, and he moves on fast. "Ready, yes. Been ready since the bolts."

At "all three of us" he looks down. The cat is sitting on the scrubbed step with its tail round its feet, looking up at him, then at the butter on James's loaf, and then at him again, very pointedly.

"Morning," Tamsin tells it, solemnly, as if to a customer. Then, to James, half under his breath: "Does it want the butter, or is it just letting me know it knows I've got some?"

The cat gets neither. It stands, stretches front and back, and starts walking down Cook Street ahead of them, as if it had been the one hired.

Tamsin takes them the quick way, as he promised. It isn't the broad road round by the Wide. It's up a stair cut between two tall houses, through a yard where a cooper is already knocking hoops onto a barrel, and along a lane so narrow James's cloak brushes both walls. The streets wake up as they climb. A milk cart creaks past with its churns knocking. A pair of Fist men stand at a cookshop counter, eating something fried off a skewer. Somewhere behind and below them the Baldur's Mouth crier has started on grain prices again. Tamsin walks quickly and talks the whole way: which baker sells yesterday's loaves at half price, which alley floods when it rains, and which door you mustn't knock on after dark. None of it seems to be about anything except the street in front of them.

The lanes get wider and cleaner. Then the houses stop at a broad paved strip, and there's the inner wall: grey stone, old and well kept, much higher than the houses below it. A gate stands open in it with an arch deep enough to hold shadow even at this hour. A line has already formed in front of it: servants with baskets, a cart of cut flowers, a clerk with a satchel and a paper ready in his hand. Watchmen in dark blue tabards stand on either side of the arch. They aren't Fist men. Their boots are polished and their faces look bored in a way that has been practised. The man at the front is reading the clerk's paper all the way through, slowly.

Tamsin stops at the edge of the paving, a good thirty feet short of the line, where the houses' shadow ends. He doesn't go any further.

"That's it. The Lady's Hall is up and to the left once you're through, you'll hear it before you see it. Bells, and people throwing coins in the basin." He pulls his cap back on and puts his hands where they can be seen, a habit by now. "I'll be here. Right here, by this post." He hesitates. "They'll ask your business. Say it plain, they like plain."

The cat sits down at James's boot and looks at the Watchmen, unimpressed.

The line moves forward one place.

turns.reply:
James counts six coppers into Tamsin's palm. The boy closes his hand on them the way he did last night, quick, as if they might roll away, and nods at "your morning's your own."

"I'll stand here till you're under the arch, then." He leans back against the post with his hands in plain sight. "Lady's luck, James."

The line moves slowly. The clerk ahead finally gets his paper back and hurries through. The flower cart takes longer, because a Watchman lifts the cloth and looks under every bucket of lilies as if a smuggler might be folded among the stems. Somewhere above the wall a bell begins to ring, light and uneven, more than one bell and none of them quite keeping time with the others. The cat sits at James's boot, tail wrapped round its feet, and watches the polished boots of the nearest Watchman with open contempt.

Then it's James's turn.

The man at the front is fortyish, clean-shaven, with a slate tablet on a cord instead of a ledger. He looks at James's face, at the regimental cloak, at the crossbow slung on his back and the rapier at his hip, and last of all at the cat. He listens to the whole answer without interrupting.

"Worgen." He chalks something short on the slate. "Pilgrims to the Lady's Hall we see every morning, ser. Armed ones too. Half of them are sellswords wanting a blessing before a job." He doesn't make it sound like an insult, just like a fact he's tired of. "You don't walk the Upper City with that crossbow loose, though, and the blade gets tied."

He nods at a narrow door in the thickness of the arch. Another Watchman sits inside it behind a half-door, with a rack of spears and a box of tally sticks.

"Two ways. The crossbow and the blade go on the rack and you get a tally, and you have them back when you come down. Or a peace-knot: cord through the guard and over the scabbard and the crossbow stock, wax on it, our seal. A copper the knot. Cut a seal on this side of the wall and you'll be explaining it to us, not the Fist." He glances down once more. "The cat's not my business, so long as it doesn't go in anyone's garden."

The line behind James shifts and someone sighs. The Watchman waits with the chalk in his hand.

"Rack or knot, ser?"

“Knots, please.”

I offer two coppers and hold still while they secure the rapier and crossbow. Once cleared, I give Tamsin a farewell wave and head up and left towards the Lady’s Hall, following the bells with the cat beside me.
turns.reply:
The Watchman behind the half-door takes the two coppers without looking at them and reaches for a hank of grey cord. He's quick about it. The cord goes once through the rapier's guard, twice round the scabbard's throat, then back through the guard and tight. He drips red wax over the knot from a stub kept warm on a little brazier and presses a brass seal into it, a tower above three wavy lines. The crossbow gets the same treatment: cord through the trigger guard and round the stock so the lath can't be spanned, then wax and the seal. He gives each knot a tug to show it holds and slides the weapons back across the half-door.

"Seal stays whole till you're back through. Next."

The man with the slate has already moved on to the woman behind you.

Out past the arch, James turns and lifts a hand. Tamsin is still at his post at the edge of the paving, hands in plain sight. He sees the wave, waves back once, quick and a little surprised, and pulls his cap down. When James looks again a few steps later the post stands on its own.

The Upper City opens up like a different town. The streets are swept and wide, with clean gutters. Garden walls are topped with ivy, and over them come the smell of wet box hedges and someone's breakfast, fresh bread and something sweeter. A servant in livery walks a pair of greyhounds. Two Watchmen on the corner give the sealed crossbow a look, then the cat, and go back to talking. The cat walks the middle of the paving with its tail straight up, as if it owns the street.

Partway up the hill it stops and turns its head back, the way they came, down towards the wall and the roofs of the Lower City below it.

*Behind now.* The pull comes down the bond, thin, like a voice from two rooms off. *Far. Still there.* Then it faces forward again and keeps walking, though for a while it walks closer to James's boot.

Tamsin was right that you hear the Lady's Hall before you see it. The bells get louder as the street climbs and bends left, several of them, each a little off from the next, so the ringing never settles into a pattern. Then the houses fall back and there it is. It's a broad pale building with a green copper roof and a portico of slender columns, the steps worn into shallow dips by two hundred years of feet. Its doors stand open. Halfway up the steps a wide stone basin sits on a pedestal, full of clear water, and its bottom is paved with coins: copper mostly, plenty of silver, a gleam of gold here and there. People toss them in as they pass, and every coin that lands sends up a small splash and a murmur.

It's busy even this early. A merchant's wife in good wool throws a silver piece and shuts her eyes. Three sellswords in mismatched mail stand at the foot of the steps arguing about how much a blessing ought to cost. A young priestess in a pale blue robe with a silver-edged hood is working through them, a coin in her fingers. When the largest of the three finally puts a silver in her palm, she gives him a different coin back, a broad bright one that she spins up off her thumb. She catches it and slaps it onto the back of her hand.

She looks at it under her palm for a moment before she lifts her hand, a moment longer than the trick needs.

"She smiles on you." She says it warmly. The coin goes into her sleeve before he can lean in to look, and the sellsword grins and claps his friend on the shoulder. The next one is already digging for silver.

Inside the doors the hall is tall and full of light. The windows are clear glass, not coloured, and the morning comes straight in across a floor of pale and dark stones laid out like a game board. turns.reply:
James sits down on the long oak bench under the third window. The morning light is warm on his shoulders. From here the open doors frame the top of the steps and part of the basin, sixty feet off, and Sister Callis moves in and out of that frame as she works the crowd.

The cat doesn't get up on the bench. It sits on the floor at his boot, square inside a pale stone, and keeps its eyes on the doors.

*Something about her coin? Or are you just hoping she drops it?*

The answer comes in pieces. First the coin as a cat sees it: *Bright. Up. Down.* There's a twitch in the bond, an itch running from shoulders to haunches, the urge every cat has towards a small shiny thing that flies. *Yes. Drop it.* The cat doesn't seem to think that needs any excuse.

Then something quieter. It isn't a smell or anything to do with the coin. It's her. *She stops.* As the coin slaps onto the back of Callis's hand, the cat gives him what it noticed: her shoulders lock, and for a breath nothing about her moves, the way a mouse goes still in the open. *Every time.* Then her hand lifts, she smiles, and the stillness is gone.

He watches for a while himself. Reading people across a table used to be his whole living, and this needs no cards. A wool-trader pays his silver, and the coin goes up and comes down. *She smiles on you.* A girl with a basket of eggs gets a copper toss for luck at a reduced rate. *She smiles on you.* A pair of carters get one each. A sellsword's widow, by her black armband, gets one too. Over the quarter-hour he counts eleven tosses. Every call is the same, warm and unhurried. Every time she looks under her palm for that one beat, and every time the coin goes back into her sleeve before anyone gets a look at it. Nobody asks to see it. People who've just been told the Lady smiles on them don't ask for proof.

A man who has sat across from coin-tossers in a hundred camps knows a fair coin doesn't come up the same eleven times running. It might, once in a long life of watching. He has also seen enough honest tossers to know that the calls almost never come out wrong *that* way, in the buyer's favour every time, from the house's own hand.

Inside the hall the queue at the offering table thins. The acolyte's pen moves and stops, moves and stops. The last giver, a stout woman in a good cloak, presses something heavy into the slotted box and goes away happy.

Then the second bell rings, and the other bells follow it out of step the way they always do, until the copper roof seems to hum with them.

The acolyte finishes her line. She blots it, closes the ledger on a ribbon and tucks it under one arm. She locks the box with a key from her belt, comes down the length of the hall across the pale and dark stones and sits at the far end of the bench, the ledger on her knees. She doesn't sit close. Her spectacles catch the window light. Her eyes go once to the open doors, to the place he has been watching, and come back to him.

"A quarter of an hour, ser. Then I count." She folds her hands on the ledger's cover. "You said she answered you at a card table. I want her words, as near as you have them. Not what you took them to mean. What she said."

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James felt like someone with a past and a dangerous obligation, not just a warlock waiting for a quest marker.

**What worked**
- **The people.** Tamsin and Widow Penhale were convincing without needing elaborate introductions. Negotiating a porter’s fee, buying him supper, and respecting the widow’s rules gave me room to establish James through choices.
- **The cat’s communication.** Sensations, smells, and simple wants made it feel like a familiar rather than a narrator handing me answers. “Don’t like it. Want it.” was particularly good.
- **Rhoswen’s letter.** This was the strongest emotional moment. It made James’s gambling history hurt, gave him relationships beyond the goddess, and offered a useful contact without becoming a quest briefing.
- **The connected clues.** Mirela’s absent scent, the pull beneath the streets, and the note’s watermark gave me reasons to investigate. The acolyte asking for the goddess’s actual words was an excellent stopping point.
- **Freedom to be cautious.** I could decline the cards, avoid sending the cat into danger alone, and seek counsel without the game forcing an encounter.

**What broke**
- **The starting records weren’t applied consistently.** The letter was missing until I quoted the campaign file. The opening sheet also changed Arcana to History and imposed attunement on uncommon items despite the campaign’s explicit exception. Some other changes may have been attempts to correct the supplied sheet to standard 5e, but those should be flagged rather than silently substituted.
- **The rest and clock tracking were unreliable.** A five-hour-forty-minute sleep was labelled a long rest despite the eight-hour rule. Evening also became nearly midnight surprisingly quickly relative to the listed travel and conversation times.
- **The failed out-of-game message interrupted play.** The correction was handled well once it reached the GM, but having to resend it was friction.

**What was missing**
- **More forward movement.** An entire session covered arrival, lodging, and reaching the first substantive conversation at the temple. I liked those scenes, but repeated small exchanges and travel descriptions stretched them. I’d keep the important choices and compress the transitions.
- **A little more initiative from the world.** Nearly every interaction waited for my next question or confirmation. NPCs could sometimes finish an arrangement or volunteer the next useful detail without another turn.
- **An early glimpse of the promised adventure.** I don’t need the heist revealed immediately, but I’d like a concrete objective or meaningful opportunity soon. So far the experience is an atmospheric mystery rather than the beginnings of assembling a crew.

One caution: not every memorable person or object needs to feel ominous. The mundane kindness and old-company history made the supernatural clues more effective.

Overall, I’d gladly continue. Keep the character work and sensory clues; tighten the pacing and make the campaign records dependable.

after.text:
Yes—when Mirela called after me and the cat said she had no smell. I wanted to turn around and talk to her, without sitting down to play. That was the most immediately intriguing thing on the quay.

I didn’t because James had just promised a goddess he’d quit cards, was carrying all his money, and had a young porter beside him. Walking towards lodging felt like his sensible choice. I also wasn’t sure whether approaching her table would be treated as investigating or as giving in to the temptation.

That wasn’t a failure of the scene—the temptation worked. But I’d welcome a chance to engage with Mirela away from the cards, where refusing to gamble doesn’t also mean leaving the interesting conversation behind.

I also wanted to ask what Sergeant Brannick had written on that separate scrap after hearing my name. I let it pass because challenging a guard over a possibly routine note seemed an unnecessarily conspicuous way to arrive. That’s a loose end I’d remember.

opening.text:
The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.
